As of 235 PM Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... There will be two potential rounds for severe 
weather today, one round through the afternoon across eastern 
counties, with a second round during the late afternoon and evening 
focused (but not limited to) western counties.

While scattered thunderstorms were expected to develop along the I-
95 corridor this afternoon, the convective temperature was reached 
slightly earlier than expected, resulting in a scattered line of 
thunderstorms along the I-95 corridor that has prompted Severe 
Thunderstorm Warnings and continues to move slowly to the east. 
Although there is a threat for large hail to the northeast of the 
Triangle, the primary threat will come from damaging winds - so far, 
all reports received had been from wind damage. Current MUCAPE 
values are between 1500-2500 J/kg, although effective wind shear 
remains less than 30 kt. Another line of showers and thunderstorms 
is expected to develop late this afternoon along the east side of 
the Appalachians and move into the area around sunset, providing the 
primary threat for damaging wind across the western part of the 
forecast area. Despite occurring at a less favorable time of day in 
terms of heating, many members of the 12Z HREF show better 
organization with the evening convection and show the potential for 
it to make its way across the forecast area, reaching the I-95 
corridor by late evening. The primary threat for severe weather with 
the second line would also be from damaging winds, and should come 
to an end shortly after midnight.

Key message 2... Today will be the last day in this stretch with 
above normal temperatures before the air mass moderates, bringing 
temperatures closer to normal.

A heat advisory remains in effect for the majority of the forecast 
area through 8pm. Heat index values remain at or above heat advisory 
criteria through much of the area where thunderstorms have not 
occurred. As of 2pm, the temperature was 95 degrees at RDU which had 
remained dry, but approximately 10 miles southeast at the NWS 
Raleigh office, which had about a third of an inch of rain, the high 
temperature reached 95 before the temperature fell to 73 degrees. In 
this sense, the area reaching heat advisory criteria will not be 
uniform.

KEY MESSAGE 3... Widespread heavy to torrential rainfall Friday 
afternoon through the early overnight hours increase the risk for 
scattered flash flooding, especially in urban and poor drainage 
locations.

A slow moving and baggy trough will largely remain in place over the 
eastern CONUS with a weakening within the trough axis extending down 
into the panhandle of FL. Weak high pressure is expected to build 
over southern Ontario and extend down through the Mid-Atlantic and 
push a weak cold front into the Carolinas by Fri morning. This 
frontal boundary will likely remain in place through the morning and 
into the afternoon as the disturbance over FL lifts north-northeast 
and into the Carolinas by the afternoon hours. 

A weak area of low pressure is expected to develop over the Midlands 
of SC as the disturbance begins to approach the synoptic boundary at 
the surface. This should act to focus low-lvl convergence and 
provide the initiating boundary for convection to develop late 
morning into the early afternoon. Surface dew points in the low/mid 
70s are expected south of this boundary and will likely support at 
least 1500-2500 SBCAPE. Tall and "skinny" CAPE profiles within an 
air mass characterized by PWAT of 2-2.3" and slow corfidi vectors 
will promote a highly favorable environment for torrential rainfall 
with a conditional risk for training, slow moving storm clusters 
surrounding meso-highs produced from prior convection. 

HREF and REFS LPMM fields show the potential for a corridor of 
widespread 1-3", surrounding the area of the frontal boundary, with 
localized amounts of +5". This corridor will be highly sensitive to 
where the boundary ends up Fri afternoon, which could be further 
complicated by more widespread convection this afternoon (Thurs 
8/20) that may affect the placement and degree of destabilization of 
the warm sector on Fri. Another potential mitigating factor for 
greater coverage of the higher-end totals will be that instability 
may be too strong during the afternoon and provide strong outflow 
that rapidly spreads away from the initiating boundary and results 
in more progressive storm clusters. Even so, impressive rain rates 
of 2-4"/hr will still drive a concern for poor drainage and urban 
flash flooding, which may occur quickly. 

Loosely organized storms within 20-30kt of 0-6km shear may support 
some organization along common cold-pools to increase the risk for 
damaging straight-line winds, but given the widespread nature of 
convection expected along the initiating boundary, wet-microburst 
within and surrounding storm collisions will be more likely and 
support 40-60 mph wind gusts and isolated instances of hail
